fields.title: The First Letter of Peter
fields.subtitle: Petrou A, “First of Peter”
fields.description: A letter of hope from the apostle Peter, sent from “Babylon”, most likely Rome, to believers scattered through Asia Minor who were being slandered and made to feel they did not belong: “Out of his great mercy he has given us a new birth.” An inheritance that can never decay, kept safe in heaven; faith tested like gold; a call to be holy, ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ; living stones built into God’s house, a chosen people and a royal priesthood; Christ who suffered for us and left a pattern to follow, by whose bruises we are healed; a ready answer for the hope within; the fiery trial, the Chief Shepherd, and a roaring lion to stand against. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the First Letter of Peter?
qa.answer: The twenty-first book of the New Testament, a letter of encouragement to Christians in the Roman provinces of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, in what is now Turkey. Most of them were Gentile converts who were slandered and mistreated by their neighbours for their new faith. Peter reminds them of the living hope they have through Christ’s resurrection, tells them they are God’s own people, and shows them how to live well, do good and endure suffering as Christ did. He sums up his purpose in 5:12: to encourage them and testify that this is the true grace of God.

qa.question: Who wrote 1 Peter, and when?
qa.answer: The letter names the apostle Peter as its author and says it was written “through Silvanus” (5:12), who may have helped write it or carried it. It sends greetings from “Babylon”, which most readers take to mean Rome. The early church accepted it as Peter’s without dispute, and Polycarp quotes it early in the second century. If Peter wrote it, it dates from the early 60s, shortly before his death in Rome under Nero. Some scholars, pointing to its polished Greek, think it was written in his name by his followers in Rome some years later.

qa.question: Why does 1 Peter call Christians foreigners and exiles?
qa.answer: Peter calls his readers people who “live as foreigners” (1:1) and “outsiders and temporary residents” (2:11), using words for people living away from home without the rights of citizens. Many of his readers were already treated as outsiders by their neighbours because of their faith. Peter tells them that this is, in a deeper sense, true: their real home and inheritance are with God, so they can live in this world honourably and without fear, as a people who belong to him.

qa.question: What does it mean that Christ preached to the spirits in prison?
qa.answer: First Peter 3:18–20 says that Christ, put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit, “went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison”, who had disobeyed in the days of Noah. It is one of the hardest passages in the New Testament, and Christians have read it in several ways: as Christ preaching through Noah to the people of his time, as Augustine thought; as Christ going to the realm of the dead between his death and resurrection; or, as many scholars now think, as the risen Christ announcing his victory to rebellious spiritual powers. All agree on Peter’s main point, that Christ now reigns over every power.

qa.question: What does 1 Peter say about suffering?
qa.answer: More than almost any other book of the New Testament, 1 Peter is about suffering. It teaches that trials test and refine faith like gold in fire (1:6–7), that suffering for doing good follows the example of Christ, who suffered for us (2:21), that believers should not be surprised by a “fire” of trial but rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings (4:12–13), and that suffering lasts only “for a little while” before God himself restores and strengthens his people (5:10).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! Out of his great mercy he has given us a new birth. Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead he has brought us into a hope that is alive, and into an inheritance that can never decay, never be stained, and never wither. That inheritance is kept safe in heaven for you, and God’s power is keeping you under guard through faith until the salvation that stands ready to be revealed at the last time.

— 1 Peter 1:3–5

First Peter is a letter of hope written to people who were being made to feel they did not belong. Its readers had turned from the gods of their towns to the God of Israel, and their neighbours had noticed. They were slandered, mocked, treated as wrongdoers, and some of them, slaves and wives in unbelieving households, were suffering for their faith inside their own homes. Peter does not promise them that it will stop. He tells them who they are, what is waiting for them, and how to live in the meantime.

It is a short letter, but a full one. In five chapters it touches almost every great theme of the New Testament: new birth, the cross and the resurrection, baptism, the church as God’s people, holiness, the Christian household, the end of all things. Every one of them is turned toward a single purpose, written in its last lines: to encourage, and to testify that this is the true grace of God.

From Peter, through Silvanus

The letter opens “From Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ”. Near the end Peter calls himself “an elder with you, a witness of the sufferings of Christ”. He says he has written “through Silvanus”, the Silas who travelled with Paul, and he sends greetings from “my son Mark” and from “She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you”. Most readers take that to be the church at Rome, called by the name of the great city of exile, as Revelation seems to do too. Eusebius, quoting the second-century bishop Papias, says the same.

The church received the letter as Peter’s from the beginning. Polycarp of Smyrna, writing early in the second century, quotes it again and again, and Eusebius counted it among the books no one disputed. Tradition holds that Peter died in Rome under Nero, in the mid-60s, so the letter would date from shortly before. Some modern scholars, noting its polished Greek and wondering whether a Galilean fisherman could have written it, think it came from a circle of Peter’s followers in Rome a decade or two after his death. Others answer that the phrase “through Silvanus” may mean that Silvanus helped write it, as secretaries often did, or simply that he carried it.

To exiles in Asia Minor

The letter is sent to God’s chosen people “who live as foreigners, scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia”, Roman provinces covering much of what is now northern and western Turkey. The list may trace the route the messenger was to take.

Its readers were mostly Gentiles. Peter speaks of “the useless way of living you inherited from your forefathers”, and reminds them that they once spent their time “doing as the pagans please”. Yet he addresses them with the titles of Israel, and calls them exiles of the dispersion. That is the heart of the letter’s comfort. The people around them treated them as outsiders. Peter tells them that is exactly what they are, “outsiders and temporary residents” in this world, because their home and their inheritance are elsewhere, kept safe in heaven.

The shape of the letter

  • 1:1–2:10: a chosen people with a living hope. New birth, an inheritance that cannot decay, a call to be holy, and a people built as living stones into God’s house.
  • 2:11–4:11: living well among outsiders. Honourable conduct before neighbours and rulers; slaves, wives and husbands; Christ’s example in suffering; and life in the light of the end.
  • 4:12–5:14: the fiery trial. Sharing Christ’s sufferings with joy, shepherds for the flock, humility, watchfulness, and greetings.

A living hope

The letter begins with praise. God, in his great mercy, has given his people a new birth, and the resurrection of Jesus has brought them into “a hope that is alive”. Their trials are real, and they hurt, but they are “for a little while”, and they are testing a faith worth more than gold. Then Peter writes one of the most tender sentences in the New Testament, to people who, unlike him, had never seen Jesus:

You have never seen him, yet you love him. You do not see him even now, but you believe in him, and you are overjoyed with a joy that words cannot express, a joy already filled with glory, because you are receiving what your faith aims at: the salvation of your souls.

— 1 Peter 1:8–9

Even the prophets searched into this salvation, Peter says, and “Even angels long to bend down and look into these things.”

Holy, ransomed, born anew

Hope is not idle. “So brace your minds for action and stay clear-headed.” God’s people are to be holy, because he is holy, and to live in reverent fear, because of what their freedom cost:

If you call on God as Father, the one who judges each person by what they have done and shows no favoritism, then live in fear of him for as long as you are strangers far from home. For you know the price of your release from the useless way of living you inherited from your forefathers. That price was not silver or gold, things that decay, but the precious blood of Christ, who was like a lamb without flaw or stain. God knew him before the world was made, and in this final age he has made him known for your sake. It is through him that you trust in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory. So your faith and hope are fixed on God.

— 1 Peter 1:17–21

They have been born anew through the living word of God. Human glory is like grass that withers. “But the word of the Lord lasts forever.”

Living stones

In chapter 2 Peter draws on a cluster of Old Testament passages about a stone: the stone God lays in Zion, the stone the builders rejected, the stone people trip over. Jesus is that stone, and those who come to him become living stones themselves, built into a house for the Spirit and serving as a holy priesthood. Then Peter gives them, Gentiles though most of them were, the titles God gave Israel at Sinai and in the prophets:

But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people God has claimed as his own, so that you may declare the great deeds of the one who called you out of the darkness into his amazing light. At one time you were no people at all; now you are God’s people. You had been shown no mercy; now God has shown you mercy.

— 1 Peter 2:9–10

Luther drew from these verses his teaching of the priesthood of all believers: every Christian may come to God directly through Christ, and every Christian has something to offer.

Doing good among those who speak against you

The middle of the letter asks how such a people should live among neighbours who distrust them. Peter’s answer is: honourably, so that those who slander them may see their good works and glorify God. They are to respect the emperor and the governors, “Give honor to every person”, and live as free people who are slaves of God.

Then he speaks to the members of a household, as other New Testament letters do. Household slaves are to bear even unjust treatment patiently. Wives are to submit to their husbands, so that unbelieving husbands may be won over without a word, by their conduct and “a gentle and quiet spirit”. Husbands are to live with their wives with understanding and honour them as fellow heirs of “the grace of life”. Christians read these instructions in different ways. Some take them as a lasting pattern for marriage and the home. Others stress how they answer a particular world, in which a wife or slave was expected to share the religion of the head of the house, and in which Peter’s concern was that the gospel not be slandered. Readers of every view notice how much he says to those with the least power, and that he speaks to them directly, as people able to choose their own conduct before God.

And to the slaves, the most vulnerable of all, Peter gives his most beautiful words about Jesus, drawn from Isaiah 53:

He himself carried our sins in his own body up onto the cross, so that we would be done with sins and live for righteousness. By the bruises he bore you have been healed. For you used to wander like lost sheep, but now you have come back to the shepherd who watches over your souls.

— 1 Peter 2:24–25

Ready to give a reason

If believers suffer for doing what is right, they are blessed. They are not to fear their opponents but to “set Christ apart as the holy Lord” in their hearts, and to be ready to make their defence to anyone who asks the reason for their hope, “with gentleness and with reverence for God.” Christ suffered too, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring them to God.

Here comes the most puzzling passage in the letter. Put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit, Christ “went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison, who had disobeyed long before” in the days of Noah (3:19–20). Who were they, and what did he proclaim? Augustine thought Peter meant that Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day. A long tradition, reflected in the creeds’ “he descended to the dead”, has seen Christ going to the realm of the dead between his death and resurrection. Many scholars today think of the rebellious spirits of Genesis 6, and of Christ, risen, announcing his victory over them. Whatever the answer, Peter’s point is clear: Christ is now at God’s right hand, and “angels, authorities, and powers have been made subject to him.”

The fiery trial

“The end of all things is near.” So Peter calls for clear heads, prayer, hospitality without grumbling, and above all love, “because love covers a great many sins.” Every gift is to be used in service, “as good managers of the richly varied grace of God.”

The trials may come like fire. They should not be surprised by it. To be insulted for the name of Christ is to have the Spirit of glory resting on them, and to suffer “for being a Christian” is no shame. It is one of only three times the New Testament uses that name.

The letter ends with a word to the elders, from one who had once been told by the lake to feed Christ’s sheep: tend the flock willingly, not for money, not as overlords, and the Chief Shepherd will give them a crown of glory. Then a word to all: put on humility, throw every worry onto God, stay awake, and stand firm against the devil, who prowls “like a lion that roars”.

How to read 1 Peter

Read it at a sitting, as a letter from a pastor to frightened people, and listen for three words that keep returning: hope, suffering and grace. Notice how often Peter turns from suffering to glory, and from the believer’s suffering to Christ’s. Notice too how he quotes the Old Testament, the Psalms, Isaiah, Exodus, Proverbs, as though it had been written for these Gentile believers, which, he says, in a sense it was (1:12).

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 1 Peter are worth knowing about before you begin.

Foreigners and outsiders. Peter uses a family of words for people living away from home without the rights of citizens. The translation keeps the picture plain: “foreigners” (1:1), “strangers far from home” (1:17), “outsiders and temporary residents” (2:11).

“The bruises he bore.” In 2:24, where older Bibles say “by whose stripes”, the translation reads “By the bruises he bore you have been healed”, keeping the language of Isaiah 53 in a form a modern reader can picture.

“The weaker vessel.” In 3:7 the translation keeps Peter’s own image, and its notes explain it as weaker in physical strength and in social power, not in mind, faith or worth. The same sentence calls the wife one “who will inherit the grace of life together with you.”

Baptism as a pledge. In 3:21 the translation reads baptism as “the pledge of a good conscience made to God”, a commitment made to God, rather than a request to him, as some Bibles have it.

“Christ.” The Open Word Bible lets a reader choose whether Christos reads “Christ” or “the Messiah”. This edition prints “Christ”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 1 Peter 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to those God has chosen who live as foreigners, scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. God the Father chose you as he knew beforehand, and the Spirit set you apart, so that you would obey Jesus Christ and be sprinkled with his blood. May grace and peace be yours in ever greater measure.

Born again into a living hope

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! Out of his great mercy he has given us a new birth. Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead he has brought us into a hope that is alive, and into an inheritance that can never decay, never be stained, and never wither. That inheritance is kept safe in heaven for you, and God’s power is keeping you under guard through faith until the salvation that stands ready to be revealed at the last time. This is why you are overjoyed, even though for a little while now, if it must be so, you have been distressed by trials of many kinds. They come so that your faith, once tested and shown to be genuine, may be found to bring praise and glory and honor at the time Jesus Christ is revealed. Faith like that is worth far more than gold, and gold perishes, even though it too is tested by fire. You have never seen him, yet you love him. You do not see him even now, but you believe in him, and you are overjoyed with a joy that words cannot express, a joy already filled with glory, because you are receiving what your faith aims at: the salvation of your souls.

What the prophets searched for

This salvation is what the prophets looked into, searching it out with great care, when they prophesied about the grace God meant for you. They tried to learn what time, and what sort of time, was being shown to them by the Spirit of Christ who was in them, as the Spirit told beforehand of the sufferings in store for Christ and the glories to come after them. God showed the prophets that what they spoke of was not for their own benefit; they were serving you. Those same things have now been reported to you by the people who brought you the good news through the Holy Spirit, who was sent from heaven. Even angels long to bend down and look into these things.

Be holy

So brace your minds for action and stay clear-headed. Put your hope entirely on the grace that is coming to you when Jesus Christ is revealed. Live as children who obey. Do not let yourselves be shaped by the desires you used to follow back when you did not know any better. Instead, be holy yourselves in all your conduct, just as the one who called you is holy, because it is written, “You are to be holy, because I am holy.”

Ransomed by precious blood

If you call on God as Father, the one who judges each person by what they have done and shows no favoritism, then live in fear of him for as long as you are strangers far from home. For you know the price of your release from the useless way of living you inherited from your forefathers. That price was not silver or gold, things that decay, but the precious blood of Christ, who was like a lamb without flaw or stain. God knew him before the world was made, and in this final age he has made him known for your sake. It is through him that you trust in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory. So your faith and hope are fixed on God.

The word that lasts forever

Now that you have made yourselves pure by obeying the truth, so that you have a genuine love for your brothers and sisters, keep loving one another from the heart with all your strength. You have been born anew, not from a seed that dies but from one that cannot die, through the word of God, which is alive and lasts. For “all people are like grass, and all their glory is like a wildflower. The grass dries up and the flower drops off. But the word of the Lord lasts forever.” And that word is the good news that was announced to you.

fields.title: 1 Peter 2
fields.body_html:
Craving the pure milk

So rid yourselves of all malice and every kind of deceit, of pretending and envy and all slander. Like newborn babies, crave the pure milk of God’s word, so that by it you may grow up into salvation, now that you have tasted that the Lord is kind.

The living stone and God’s own people

You come to him, the living stone that people rejected as worthless but God chose and prizes. And you yourselves, as living stones, are being built up as a house for the Spirit, to serve as a holy priesthood and to offer, through Jesus Christ, spiritual sacrifices that God gladly accepts. For this is what Scripture says: “See, I am placing in Zion a stone, a cornerstone, chosen and precious, and no one who believes in him will ever be put to shame.” So the honor belongs to you who believe. But for those who do not believe, “The very stone the builders rejected has become the main cornerstone,” and “a stone they trip over, a rock that brings them down.” They trip because they refuse to obey the word, and this is the end to which they were appointed.

But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people God has claimed as his own, so that you may declare the great deeds of the one who called you out of the darkness into his amazing light. At one time you were no people at all; now you are God’s people. You had been shown no mercy; now God has shown you mercy.

Good lives among those who do not know God

Dear friends, you live here as outsiders and temporary residents. So I urge you to keep away from the cravings of the flesh, for they fight against your soul. Let your way of life among those who do not know God be honorable. Then, though they speak against you as wrongdoers, they will see your good works for themselves and glorify God on the day he visits.

Free people under human authority

For the Lord’s sake, place yourselves under every authority that people have set up: the emperor, who holds the highest rank, and the governors he sends out to punish wrongdoing and to reward good conduct with praise. For this is God’s will: that by doing good you muzzle the ignorance of foolish people. Act as free people. Your freedom is not a mask for wickedness; you are slaves who belong to God. Give honor to every person. Love your fellow believers. Fear God. Give honor to the emperor.

Suffering unjustly in the steps of Christ

Household slaves, place yourselves under your masters with deep reverence, not just those who are kind and gentle but also those who are crooked and harsh. For this finds favor: when someone, mindful of God, bears up under pain while suffering unjustly. For what is praiseworthy about putting up with blows when you have done wrong? But if you do good and suffer for it and you endure, this finds favor with God. It was for this that God called you, because Christ also suffered for you and left you a pattern to copy, so that you would walk in his footsteps. He never sinned, and no one ever found deceit in his mouth. People heaped abuse on him, yet he did not answer abuse with abuse. As he suffered, he made no threats, but went on handing himself over to the God who judges justly. He himself carried our sins in his own body up onto the cross, so that we would be done with sins and live for righteousness. By the bruises he bore you have been healed. For you used to wander like lost sheep, but now you have come back to the shepherd who watches over your souls.

fields.title: 1 Peter 3
fields.body_html:
Wives and husbands

In the same way, wives, submit to your own husbands. Then if any of them do not obey the word, your way of life will win them over even without your saying a word, as they watch how pure your conduct is and how you live in reverence for God. Do not let your adornment be the outward kind: braided hair, gold ornaments, and the clothes you put on. Let it be the hidden self of the heart, adorned with what never decays, a gentle and quiet spirit, which God values highly. This is how the holy women of the past who put their hope in God made themselves beautiful: they submitted to their own husbands. So Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him her lord. You have become her daughters, as long as you do what is good and let nothing terrify you.

Husbands, in the same way, live with your wives with understanding. Give honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, and as one who will inherit the grace of life together with you, so that nothing stands in the way of your prayers.

Blessing instead of insult

To sum up: all of you, be united in mind, share one another’s feelings, love each other as brothers and sisters, be tender in heart and humble in mind. Do not pay back evil with evil or abuse with abuse. Instead, bless, because this is what you were called to, so that you may inherit a blessing. For whoever wants to love life and see good days must hold back the tongue from evil and the lips from speaking deceit, must turn away from evil and do good, must look for peace and go after it. For the Lord keeps his eyes on the righteous and turns his ears to their prayer, but the Lord’s face is set against those who do evil.

Suffering for doing good

And who will do you harm if you are devoted to doing what is good? But suppose you do suffer because of righteousness: even then you are blessed. Do not be afraid of what they threaten, and do not be shaken. Instead, in your hearts set Christ apart as the holy Lord. Be ready at all times to make your defense to anyone who asks you for the reason behind the hope you hold. Yet answer with gentleness and with reverence for God, keeping a good conscience, so that when people speak evil of you, those who insult your good life in Christ will be ashamed. It is better, after all, to suffer while doing good, if God wills that, than to suffer while doing wrong. For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous one for the unrighteous, so that he might lead you to God. In the flesh he was put to death, but in the spirit he was made alive. In that spirit he also went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison, who had disobeyed long before, when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In that ark a few people, eight in all, came safely through the water. This water points ahead to baptism, which now saves you as well. Baptism is not washing dirt off the body, but the pledge of a good conscience made to God. It saves you through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. He went into heaven and is now at God’s right hand, and angels, authorities, and powers have been made subject to him.

fields.title: 1 Peter 4
fields.body_html:
Living for the will of God

So then, since Christ suffered in the body, you too must arm yourselves with the same resolve, because whoever has suffered in the body is done with sin. Then you will spend the rest of your time in the body living no longer for human desires but for what God wills. For the time that is behind you was enough for doing as the pagans please: a life of sensuality and lust, drunkenness, wild feasts, drinking parties and forbidden idol worship. They are surprised that you no longer plunge with them into the same flood of wild and wasteful living, and so they speak evil of you. They will answer for this to the one who stands ready to judge both the living and the dead. This is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead: so that, though by human reckoning they were judged in the body, by God’s reckoning they might live in the spirit.

Good managers of God’s grace

The end of all things is near. So be sensible and keep a clear head for the sake of your prayers. Most important of all, keep your love for one another strong and unfailing, because love covers a great many sins. Welcome one another into your homes without complaining. Each of you has received a gift; use it to serve one another, as good managers of the richly varied grace of God. Whoever speaks must speak as one bringing God’s own words. Whoever serves must serve in the strength God supplies. Then in everything God will be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and power forever and ever. Amen.

Suffering as a Christian

Dear friends, the fire that is burning among you has come to test you; do not be taken aback by it, as though something alien to you were happening. No, the more you share in the sufferings of Christ, the more you should rejoice, so that you may also rejoice with shouts of joy when his glory is revealed. If you are insulted because you bear the name of Christ, you are blessed, since the Spirit of glory, the very Spirit of God, rests on you. Of course, none of you should suffer for being a murderer or a thief or a criminal, or even for interfering in other people’s affairs. But if someone suffers for being a Christian, they should feel no shame, but should give glory to God by bearing this name. For now is the time for judgment to start, and it starts at God’s own house. If we are the first to face it, how will it end for those who refuse to obey God’s gospel? And, “If the righteous are saved only with difficulty, what place will there be for the godless and the sinner?” So, then, those who suffer as God wills should place themselves in the hands of the Creator, who is faithful, while they keep on doing what is good.

fields.title: 1 Peter 5
fields.body_html:
Shepherds of God’s flock

So I appeal to the elders among you. I am an elder with you, a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and one who will also share in the glory that is about to be revealed. Tend God’s flock among you as shepherds do. Take care of it freely, the way God would have it, not because you are forced to; not to make money for yourselves, but gladly and readily. Do not rule harshly over the people given into your charge; set an example for the flock instead. Then when the Chief Shepherd is revealed, you will be given a crown of glory that will never wither. In the same way, you who are younger, submit to the elders. And all of you, tie humility on like a garment in your dealings with one another, because “God stands against the arrogant, but he gives grace to the humble.”

Humble under God’s hand

Humble yourselves, then, under God’s powerful hand, so that he may raise you up when the time is right. Do this by throwing every worry you have onto him, because you matter to him. Keep a clear head. Stay awake. The devil, your opponent, roams about like a lion that roars, hunting for someone to swallow up. Stand up to him and hold firm in your faith. You know that your brothers and sisters all over the world are enduring these same sufferings. And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore you, make you firm and strong, and set you on a sure foundation. Power belongs to him forever and ever. Amen.

Final greetings

I have written you this short letter through Silvanus, whom I count a faithful brother. I write to encourage you and to testify that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, and so does my son Mark. Greet each other with a loving kiss. May all of you who belong to Christ have peace.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore you, make you firm and strong, and set you on a sure foundation.

— 1 Peter 5:10

First Peter never pretends that suffering is small. It speaks of trials by fire, of slander and blows, of a devil who roars. But it measures all of it with one phrase: “for a little while”. Set against an inheritance that never withers and a God of all grace who has called his people to eternal glory, even the fiery trial is short. And the God who allows it is the one who will restore, strengthen and establish them himself.

The question the letter leaves

The question Peter leaves is how to live as an outsider without becoming bitter. His readers could have hardened into a resentful little group, hitting back at those who mocked them, or they could have quietly given in and gone back to their old ways. Peter shows them a third way, the way of Christ, who “did not answer abuse with abuse” but handed himself over to the God who judges justly. They are to bless instead of curse, to do good, to stay ready with a gentle answer for their hope, and to let their lives speak.

That way is not weakness. It takes a settled confidence in God to throw every worry onto him and still stand firm against the devil. Peter had learned that the hard way, on the night he denied his Lord by a fire in a courtyard. The man who writes “Stand up to him and hold firm in your faith” is a man who once did not, and was restored.

Where the letter points

It points forward, to the day “when Jesus Christ is revealed”, a phrase Peter returns to again and again. Hope, in this letter, is not wishful thinking but something solid, an inheritance kept in heaven for people kept by God’s power.

And it points to the church: a spiritual house of living stones, a holy priesthood, a flock with shepherds who serve gladly, and a family of brothers and sisters all over the world who are going through the same sufferings. No one in this letter suffers alone.

Where to go from here

First Peter has comforted the suffering church in every century, and many of its interpreters are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the living hope (1:3–9). Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s A Living Hope of the Hereafter (1:3–4); Andrew Murray’s Kept by the Power of God (1:5), in Absolute Surrender; John Wesley’s Heaviness through Manifold Temptations (1:6), in Sermons on Several Occasions; and Jonathan Edwards’s Religious Affections, which takes 1:8 as its text.
  • On holiness (1:15–16). Murray’s Holy in Christ, a month of readings on the call to be holy as God is holy.
  • On Christ the stone and the shepherd (chapter 2). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Christ Precious to Believers (2:7); his The Sin-Bearer (2:24), in Till He Come; and Hudson Taylor’s Under the Shepherd’s Care (2:25).
  • On Christ suffering for sins (3:18). John Flavel’s The Saints Brought Home to God, in The Method of Grace.
  • On humility under God’s hand (5:5–7). Thomas Boston’s The Crook in the Lot, which includes a sermon on 5:6, and Murray’s Humility, whose chapter Humility and Exaltation takes up the same verse.
  • On Peter and the churches he wrote to. The Epistle and Martyrdom of Polycarp, from a bishop in the province of Asia who quoted this letter often and died for his faith; The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, sent from Rome a generation later, which remembers Peter’s witness and death; and Eusebius of Caesarea’s The Church History.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 1 Peter in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read the letter again, the next time life feels like a fiery trial, and to hear it as its first readers did: as a word from someone who had suffered and failed and been restored, and who knew that the grace he wrote about was true. Peter’s last words are a blessing:

May all of you who belong to Christ have peace.

— 1 Peter 5:14
